notes: Friday 6 Nov 2026 world issue (Taipei ~08:00). Window: Thu 5 Nov (two days after US midterms). Economy: Nasdaq −5.5% AI scare; BoE hikes to 4%; poor-country debt $9.4tn; Mag7 −$1tn / Musk names −$420bn. Tech (USA): OpenAI data-center pledges; Dems push moratorium; tech barons after blue wave; Musk midterm flop. Politics: Dems to-do list; Joshua Wong 10 years; Paraguay president quits bank crash; Newsom clears death row. Literature: Min Jin Lee HOT; Goncourt AI NOT; Miéville Goldsmiths HOT; Rogoyska Paris award HOT. Social: abortion ballots; Europe bomb hoaxes; France strikes; teens exercise gap.

stories.headline: Nasdaq has worst day in 18 months (−5.5%); Dow −3.4% as markets fear AI slowdown after Democrat wins
stories.dek: Chip stocks lead crash. SanDisk −22%, Western Digital −17%. VIX fear index jumps 61%.
stories.caveman: On Thursday, US tech stocks got crushed. The Nasdaq fell about 5.5% — worst day in 18 months — and entered ‘correction’ (more than 10% below its recent high). More than $2 trillion of Nasdaq value vanished in one day. The Dow fell over 1,800 points (−3.4%); S&P 500 fell about 4.3%. Why? Investors bet Democrats winning Congress and many governor races means tougher rules on AI data centers. Memory and hard-drive stocks led the slide. Wall Street’s fear gauge (VIX) jumped 61%. This erased Wednesday’s happy post-election rally.
stories.why_it_matters: When US tech crashes, Taiwan chip and AI supply-chain stocks often follow the next morning. Pension funds and global ETFs feel it too.
stories.camps: Bulls say the selloff is overdone panic. Bears say AI spending dreams just met politics. Trump allies blame Democrats; Democrats say voters already rejected data-center sprawl.

terms.explain: US stock index heavy with tech companies.
Drop of more than 10% from a recent high.
‘Fear index’ — higher means investors expect wild swings.
Huge buildings full of computers that run AI and the cloud.
Companies that make computer chips, like Nvidia or memory makers.

stories.headline: Bank of England raises rates to 4% — first hike in over three years — warns Iran war keeps inflation hot
stories.dek: Eight of nine MPC members vote for +0.25pp. Oil stuck above $100; UK inflation may hit 4.9% mid-2027.
stories.caveman: Britain’s central bank lifted its base rate from 3.75% to 4% — first rise in more than three years. Eight policymakers said yes; one wanted an even bigger half-point jump. The Iran war kept oil expensive (often above $100 a barrel), so the Bank now thinks UK inflation could climb to 4.9% by mid-next year (it was 3.5% in September). Governor Andrew Bailey said another hike is possible unless the war cools, but this is not the start of an endless hiking cycle. Higher rates hurt people with mortgages; savers get a bit more interest.
stories.why_it_matters: UK rates affect global money flows and the pound. Cost-of-living pain also shapes politics in a big democracy.
stories.camps: Hawks say fight inflation first. Doves say households already hurt. Markets watch the Dec 17 meeting and oil news.
stories.image_alt: Bank of England / interest rate decision

terms.explain: The central bank’s main interest rate that guides loans and savings.
Monetary Policy Committee — the group that votes on UK rates.
Prices going up over time.
Home loan; higher rates usually mean bigger monthly payments.

stories.headline: Poorest countries’ debt hits record $9.4tn; World Bank says they pay highest rates since late 1980s
stories.dek: Debt up 5.5% last year — fastest in four years. Average new interest for poorest: 8.2%.
stories.caveman: The World Bank says developing countries now owe a record $9.4 trillion. Debt rose 5.5% last year, fastest in four years, helped by lots of private lending. The poorest countries (ones that can get cheap World Bank loans) paid an average 8.2% interest on new borrowing — highest since the late 1980s. Examples: Laos ~11.5%, Congo ~13.9%, Kenya ~9.2%. High debt service means less money for schools, health, and food security when global shocks hit. The UK, as future G20 president, talks about a new debt drive linked partly to slavery legacy debates.
stories.why_it_matters: When poor countries drown in interest, crises can spread — migration, unrest, and unpaid loans to rich-world banks.
stories.camps: Creditors want repayment. Debtor nations and activists want relief and cheaper finance. The Bank says access improved but the price did not.
stories.image_alt: Protesters seek debt relief at IMF-World Bank meetings

terms.explain: Money a country owes to foreign lenders.
Cash spent just to pay interest and principal.
Group of 20 big economies that meet on global rules.
Loans with softer terms for poorer countries.

stories.headline: Magnificent 7 lose about $1tn in one day; Musk’s Tesla + SpaceX shed $420bn+ after midterms
stories.dek: AI selloff + fear of probes and data-center rules hit the richest tech names.
stories.caveman: Thursday’s rout was huge in dollar terms. CNBC tallied that the ‘Magnificent 7’ mega-tech group lost about $1 trillion in market value. Separately, Elon Musk’s Tesla (about −11%) and SpaceX (about −9%) together lost over $420 billion in market value since Tuesday’s close. Forbes says Musk’s fortune fell from over $1 trillion toward under $800 billion. He spent roughly $470 million backing Republicans — most of his picks lost. Democrats now control Congress; in Texas, new Democratic leaders criticize big data centers. Investors fear probes and tighter rules for Musk companies.
stories.why_it_matters: Paper wealth swings this big move indexes, retirement funds, and the mood for AI investment worldwide — including Taiwan’s supply chain.
stories.camps: Musk allies call it temporary politics. Critics say voters rejected oligarch spending. Traders just see risk and hit sell.

terms.explain: Nickname for a handful of giant US tech stocks that drove recent bull markets.
Company value = share price × number of shares.
US elections halfway through a president’s term.

stories.headline: OpenAI pledges: pay full power costs, no NDAs with officials, publish plans after voters reject data centers
stories.dek: Local ballots: voters backed limits on almost all of 41 measures across 10 states.
stories.caveman: Two days after election day, OpenAI put out promises for the data centers it owns: pay the full cost of electricity, ask communities for input, publish construction plans, and stop using non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) that keep deals secret from the public. It also floated a policy blueprint for lawmakers. Meta, Microsoft, Google and Anthropic have floated similar ideas. On Tuesday, Ballotpedia-style tallies showed voters backed restrictions or rejected pro-build measures in all but one of 41 local data-center ballots across 10 states. People worried about water, power bills, jobs, and AI anxiety.
stories.why_it_matters: AI needs giant computer barns. If towns keep saying no — and companies change rules — build speed and chip demand can slow.
stories.camps: OpenAI says this is a ‘high floor’ of good behavior. Activists want laws, not promises. Industry fears delays.

terms.explain: Non-disclosure agreement — a secrecy contract.
A yes/no question voters decide directly on election day.
A suggested plan for rules, not yet law.

stories.headline: Top Democrats push to rein in AI buildout: Sanders calls for ‘national data center moratorium now’
stories.dek: 56% of CNBC poll voters said AI/data centers were a big vote factor; chip ETF SOXX −9%.
stories.caveman: After the midterm sweep, progressive Democrats moved fast on AI infrastructure. Sen. Bernie Sanders cheered local bans and posted: ‘National data center moratorium now.’ House members said pausing AI development should be Day-1 priority. CNBC’s voter poll: 56% said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor; of those, 65% backed Democrats for Congress. Chip-linked stocks sold off hard (SOXX nearly −9%; Nvidia about −8%; AMD more than −14%). Candidates who flipped races had attacked ‘data center’ opponents by name.
stories.why_it_matters: A national pause would be a huge shift for Big Tech, utilities, and Taiwan’s AI hardware orders.
stories.camps: Progressives want brakes on Big Tech. Industry warns of losing the AI race to China. Moderates may prefer local rules over a full freeze.

terms.explain: A temporary ban or freeze.
ETF that tracks many semiconductor stocks.
Left wing of the Democratic Party.

stories.headline: Tech barons knelt to Trump at inauguration — now a blue Congress looks like a hit list
stories.dek: Voters punished oligarch influence and AI sprawl; Casar: hold billionaires accountable.
stories.caveman: Photos of Musk, Bezos, Zuckerberg at Trump’s 2025 inauguration once meant power. After Democrats took Congress and many governorships — even in deep-red places like Texas — that bet looks risky. Reporting says anger at tech oligarchs, AI boom, data centers, and surveillance cameras helped drive votes. Rep. Greg Casar: voters rejected Republicans ‘bought and paid for by AI billionaires.’ Sen. Jon Ossoff blasted Silicon Valley bunker culture. Fortunes that ballooned under Maga + AI now face committees, taxes, and regulation talk.
stories.why_it_matters: Who writes the rules for AI and monopoly power will shape the next decade of tech — and Taiwan’s biggest customers.
stories.camps: Tech PR will pivot to Democrats. Populists on left and right still distrust Big Tech. Investors price political risk.

terms.explain: Extremely rich person with big political power.
Trump’s ‘Make America Great Again’ political brand.
Hardened shelter — used here as a metaphor for rich people preparing for disaster.

stories.headline: Musk spent nearly $500m on midterms — and mostly lost; analysis calls the bet a flop
stories.dek: Biggest GOP donor still saw his candidates fail as Democrats swept.
stories.caveman: Elon Musk poured nearly half a billion dollars into Republican midterm races — the biggest donor push of its kind — yet most candidates he backed lost. Analyses frame the spending as a flop: money bought ads and noise, not durable voter love. Combined with Thursday’s stock hit to Tesla and SpaceX, the political and market bill for aligning hard with Trump-era politics arrived at once. The story sits next to voter backlash against AI billionaires and data centers.
stories.why_it_matters: If money-in-politics stops working for tech titans, they may change lobbying — or double down. Either path moves policy.
stories.camps: Musk allies say one cycle isn’t destiny. Critics say voters rejected pay-to-win politics. Campaign pros study which messages failed.

terms.explain: Person or group that gives money to campaigns.
US elections in the middle of a presidential term.

stories.headline: After blue wave, Democrats sketch a long to-do list for new Congress majority
stories.dek: House + Senate control opens probes, spending fights, and checks on Trump’s last years.
stories.caveman: Democrats won both chambers. NPR and other outlets describe a long wish list: oversight of Trump-era deals, possible energy and crypto probes, abortion and health policy, and pressure on Big Tech / data centers. Some races were still counting, but the majority math looks solid enough that markets and foreign capitals are already gaming a constrained White House. Divided or opposed Congress can slow tariffs, appointments, and war policy — or spark shutdown fights.
stories.why_it_matters: US lawmaking shapes Taiwan security aid, chip rules, and global markets. A blue Congress changes the bargaining table.
stories.camps: Democratic activists want fast action. Trump allies vow resistance. Swing voters may punish chaos either way.

terms.explain: Big election win for Democrats (blue = party color).
Congress investigating and checking the executive branch.
One house of Congress: House or Senate.

stories.headline: Hong Kong’s Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years for ‘foreign collusion’ under national security law
stories.dek: Second NSL conviction; Amnesty says law is used to crush peaceful advocacy.
stories.caveman: Activist Joshua Wong — face of 2014 Umbrella protests as a teen — got 10 years after pleading guilty to ‘foreign collusion.’ Judge William Tam called his acts ‘grave,’ saying Wong sought foreign sanctions with exiled activist Nathan Law. Sentence runs with remaining time from a prior security case. Law called it crushing hope for democracy; Amnesty said the security law is a tool to punish peaceful work. Taiwan’s presidential office also condemned the verdict.
stories.why_it_matters: Hong Kong’s legal chill is a human-rights story and a warning about how ‘security’ laws can erase opposition.
stories.camps: Hong Kong authorities say courts apply the law. Rights groups call it political persecution. Democracies issue statements; leverage is limited.

terms.explain: 2020 Hong Kong law criminalizing secession, subversion, terrorism, collusion.
2014 Hong Kong democracy sit-ins.
Charge of working with outsiders against the state.

stories.headline: Paraguay president Santiago Peña quits after Ueno Bank freeze hits ~3 million savers
stories.dek: Digital bank collapse sparks protests; impeachment was already moving; VP to take over.
stories.caveman: Paraguay’s right-wing president Santiago Peña resigned after a banking crisis. Central bank put Ueno Bank into resolution; about 3 million customers — roughly 60% of adults, the bank claimed — saw deposits frozen, leaving families without grocery money. Executives were arrested; streets filled with protesters. Ueno grew fast with cash-back and soccer sponsorship, and held hundreds of millions in state and pension cash. Peña faced impeachment with broad support; he quit by video saying the republic comes first. NPR notes impeachment followed minutes after resignation in some accounts.
stories.why_it_matters: A modern ‘fintech for the masses’ failure can topple a government overnight — and wipe household savings.
stories.camps: Opposition blames cozy ties and weak supervision. Peña frames resignation as duty. Depositors just want their money.

terms.explain: Official takeover of a failing bank to wind it down or save parts.
Legislature removing a president for alleged wrongdoing.
Finance + technology apps and digital banks.

stories.headline: California’s Newsom commutes all 548 death sentences to life without parole
stories.dek: Largest modern US clearing of a death row; follows outrage over a botched Tennessee execution.
stories.caveman: Governor Gavin Newsom turned every California death sentence into life without parole — 529 men and 19 women, largest death row in the Western Hemisphere. He called state killing incompatible with justice in an imperfect system. Newsom already paused executions in 2019 and emptied the San Quentin death chamber. California has not executed anyone since 2006; many waited 15+ years. The move blocks future governors from restarting the machinery of death for these people. It also boosts Newsom’s 2028 presidential profile among progressives — and angers death-penalty supporters.
stories.why_it_matters: Capital punishment is a core human-rights fight. California’s size makes this the biggest single US shift in years.
stories.camps: Abolitionists celebrate. Victims’ families are split. Conservatives call it soft on crime. Courts still review individual cases.

terms.explain: Change a sentence to a lesser one.
Prisoners waiting under a death sentence.
Stay in prison until death; no release date.

stories.headline: HOT: Min Jin Lee’s American Hagwon — glorious, immersive follow-up to Pachinko, critics cheer
stories.dek: Guardian review: deep dive into Korean-American ambition, education factories, and family.
stories.caveman: Min Jin Lee — author of the beloved novel Pachinko — is back with American Hagwon. Early reviews call it richly immersive: a story about hagwons (private cram schools), immigrant hustle, and what ‘making it’ costs. Lee remains ‘hot’: book clubs, awards chatter, and readers who loved Pachinko want the next long visit into Korean diaspora life. If you like big character novels about class and belonging, this is the heat check of the week.
stories.why_it_matters: Who’s hot in US literary fiction often becomes what libraries buy, what book clubs read, and what gets adapted later.
stories.camps: Fans celebrate another epic. Some readers tire of ‘immigrant novel’ marketing boxes. Teachers may assign excerpts on education pressure.

terms.explain: Korean private after-school cram academy.
Min Jin Lee’s famous multi-generation Korean-Japanese epic novel.
People living outside their ancestral homeland.

stories.headline: NOT / controversy: Prix Goncourt winner admits using AI — French prize shaken
stories.dek: Philippe Jaenada’s win meets backlash after AI disclosure; ‘who wrote this?’ fight goes mainstream.
stories.caveman: France’s top literary prize, the Prix Goncourt, is in a storm: the winner admits using AI in the work. For traditionalists, that is a hard ‘not’ — prizes were meant for human craft. For others, the fight is honesty and rules, not the tool itself. Either way, the scandal is now part of US literary conversation too: journals, MFA blogs, and publishers argue what counts as authorship when machines draft sentences.
stories.why_it_matters: If major prizes blur human vs AI credit, contracts, copyright, and school honor codes all get messy.
stories.camps: Purists want bans. Experimenters want disclosure labels. Prize boards scramble to write clearer rules.

terms.explain: France’s most famous literary prize.
Who counts as the true writer of a text.
Telling readers you used a tool like AI.

stories.headline: HOT: China Miéville wins Goldsmiths Prize for 1,200-page novel The Rouse
stories.dek: £10,000 UK prize for ‘fiction that breaks the mould’; jury says he was destined for it.
stories.caveman: British novelist China Miéville — long a cult hero of weird, political, inventive fiction — won the Goldsmiths Prize for The Rouse, a 1,200-page beast. The prize rewards novels that take risks with form. Judges basically said: of course this guy. For US readers of speculative and literary experimental work, Miéville stays ‘hot’ when big prizes validate huge, strange books in an age of short attention.
stories.why_it_matters: Prizes steer what bookstores shelve face-out and what translation scouts notice.
stories.camps: Fans of door-stopper novels rejoice. Casual readers may fear the page count. Academics love teaching ‘mould-breaking’ form.

terms.explain: UK award for innovative fiction.
Stories with unreal or futuristic elements (sci-fi, fantasy-adjacent).
Slang for a very thick book.

stories.headline: HOT: Christina Rogoyska’s Hotel Exile wins 2026 American Library in Paris Book Award
stories.dek: $5,000 prize + hand-bound edition; WWII Paris history that reads like lived memory.
stories.caveman: Lit Hub reports Christina Rogoyska won the American Library in Paris Book Award for Hotel Exile: Paris in the Shadow of War. Jury (including last year’s winner Sue Prideaux, Molly Ringwald, Dan Jones) praised its spirit. Prize: $5,000 and a special hand-bound copy; another copy goes into the library’s special collections. For US/Anglophone readers who love narrative history with novelistic heat, this is a fresh ‘who’s hot’ marker from a Paris–US literary bridge.
stories.why_it_matters: Paris-based English prizes help US audiences find history books with international buzz.
stories.camps: History buffs excited. Novel purists may shrug at nonfiction winning bookish heat. Libraries expand WWII Paris shelves.
stories.image_alt: American Library in Paris Book Award

terms.explain: English-language library and cultural hub in Paris.
History written with story-like scenes and characters.
Rare or treasured books kept for research.

stories.headline: Midterm ballots protect abortion rights in Nevada and Virginia; Missouri keeps 2024 protections
stories.dek: Idaho keeps its ban. Reproductive-rights night mostly succeeds inside the blue wave.
stories.caveman: Voters decided several abortion measures. Nevada passed a constitutional right to abortion through the second trimester (then regulate after viability except for life/health). Virginia approved a ‘fundamental right to reproductive freedom’ covering abortion, contraception, and fertility care with similar trimester rules. Missouri rejected Amendment 3, which would have rolled back 2024 protections and added gender-care bans for minors. Idaho voters did not repeal that state’s ban. Overall, rights advocates call it a successful night nested in the wider Democratic wave.
stories.why_it_matters: State constitutions now matter as much as the US Supreme Court for abortion access.
stories.camps: Rights groups celebrate. Anti-abortion groups regroup for legislatures and courts. National parties will keep using the issue in 2028.

terms.explain: Law or amendment decided by voters directly.
Point when a fetus might survive outside the womb.
Change to a state constitution; hard to reverse.

stories.headline: Hoax bomb threats disrupt 25+ European flights; second wave this week sparks hybrid-war fears
stories.dek: Ryanair, Aer Lingus, Wizz and more divert; all clear so far; at least 33 flights hit this week.
stories.caveman: Fake bomb warnings hit at least 25 flights across Europe on Thursday — Italy, Ireland, UK, Spain, Bulgaria, and more. Planes diverted or searched; nothing found. Airlines included Ryanair, Aer Lingus, Wizz, Finnair, easyJet and others. Heathrow and Birmingham got threats judged hoaxes. Similar scares hit earlier in the week (total 33+ flights). Investigators have not proved a state actor like Russia or Iran, but politicians talk ‘hybrid war’ — cheap chaos without real bombs. Iata urged finding the source.
stories.why_it_matters: Even fake threats cost money, trust, and nerves — and can be used to rattle open societies.
stories.camps: Security agencies chase digital trails. Airlines want faster triage so every hoax doesn’t ground a plane. Public fear is the attacker’s product.

terms.explain: A false threat meant to scare or disrupt.
Mixing cyber, propaganda, crime, and scare tactics with or instead of open fighting.
Global airline trade group.

stories.headline: France: hundreds of thousands march as unions strike over cost of living and public-service cuts
stories.dek: Government tally ~600k; CGT union says nearly 1.6m. Teachers, nurses, rail workers, students.
stories.caveman: France saw another big protest day. Unions called a general strike; teachers, hospital staff, rail workers, and students marched in Paris and other cities. Government said at least 600,000 people; the CGT union claimed almost 1.6 million. Police presence was heavy (~70,000); tear gas in Bordeaux and Lyon. Protesters say Macron-era budget squeezes hit services while debt nears 120% of GDP. Rail unions warn cuts deepen poverty and freeze public pay.
stories.why_it_matters: Street pressure can force budget changes — or harden governments. Europe watches France’s debt vs dignity fight.
stories.camps: Unions want wages and services. Government cites debt math. Students want usable schools. Tear gas videos polarize TV audiences.

terms.explain: Many industries stop work on the same day.
Major French left-wing trade union.
Size of a country’s economy.

stories.headline: Teens worldwide still don’t move enough — girls fall even further behind, new data show
stories.dek: Global adolescent exercise gap is a quiet health emergency.
stories.caveman: NPR reports new findings: teenagers around the world still fail to get enough physical activity, and girls lag boys even more. Screens, unsafe streets, sports access, and school schedules all play roles. Experts warn lifelong risks — heart disease, mental health, bone strength — start with habits formed now. Fix ideas include safer play spaces, quality PE, and cutting the homework-vs-sport tradeoff that hits girls harder in many cultures.
stories.why_it_matters: Public health is not only hospitals; it is whether kids can run, play, and feel strong.
stories.camps: Schools say curricula are packed. Parents cite safety and time. Health agencies push PE and city design.

terms.explain: Young person roughly age 10–19.
Physical education class at school.
Difference in outcomes between girls and boys.
